name: Hot-sauce thermogenics / spicy food
lead: Hot-sauce thermogenics refers to eating chili peppers, hot sauce or capsaicin supplements in the belief that the heat speeds metabolism and helps fat loss. Capsaicin, the pungent compound in chilies, binds the TRPV1 receptor on pain-sensing nerves, producing sensations of heat [1].

Wikipedia reports that a 2007 source found no evidence linking capsaicin ingestion directly to weight loss, and a 2014 meta-analysis found weak evidence that capsaicin before a meal might slightly reduce intake [1]. Large doses can irritate and cause nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain [1].

paras: Capsaicin opens the TRPV1 ion channel on nociceptor nerve fibres, causing warmth and sometimes stinging; research on these sensors was recognised by the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine [1]. Orally it is well absorbed but extensively metabolised in the liver, with a blood half-life of about 25 minutes after a pepper extract in humans [1].

Wikipedia notes that well-designed trials have been hard to run because pungency makes doses difficult for participants to tolerate [1]. The 2014 meta-analysis suggested a small possible effect on food intake and a shift toward carbohydrate preference [1].

Capsaicin irritates skin, eyes and airways, and peppers are among the common plant exposures reported to poison centres [1]. A 2012 case report described a heart attack in a healthy 25-year-old after cayenne pepper pills, and a 2024 autopsy linked a teenager's death to a spicy chip challenge [1].
No studies found specific to hot sauce. Studies of capsaicin itself reported weak evidence of a small effect on food intake [1].

timeline.event: Christian Friedrich Bucholz first extracts capsaicin in impure form [1].
J. C. Thresh obtains nearly pure capsaicin [1].
The Qutenza capsaicin patch is approved for post-herpetic neuralgia in the US and EU [1].

card.summary: Spicy food as a metabolism booster; capsaicin may nudge appetite slightly, and weight-loss evidence is limited.
card.note: Capsaicin pills have been linked to rare serious cardiac events in case reports.

quick.overview:
Some dieters add hot sauce, chilies or capsaicin supplements hoping to raise metabolism and lose fat.

Reviews cited on Wikipedia found no direct link between capsaicin and weight loss, with weak evidence of a small effect on food intake.
quick.mechanism: Capsaicin activates the TRPV1 heat-and-pain receptor on sensory nerves. Proponents say this triggers extra heat production and reduced appetite.
quick.risks: Capsaicin can irritate the mouth, stomach, skin and eyes, causing nausea or diarrhea. Isolated case reports describe serious events from concentrated pills or extreme spicy challenges.
